# Bootstrapping experiments {#sec-bootstrapping}

The question of this book is whether word–object mapping can be **bootstrapped** from
naturalistic data — whether a learner can climb from naive contrastive training toward the
ceiling using only signal it could plausibly have. This chapter maps that climb with a single,
systematic design: train on **all** of BabyView (36 children, 911k pairs on an 80% video split),
evaluate on the out-of-sample **Konkle** benchmark (@sec-eval), and measure what each mechanism
contributes against oracle toplines. Everything is 3 seeds; the primary number is Konkle test-60.

## Three bootstraps

Every mechanism here is a form of *self-supervised selection* — deciding what to attend to
without being told the answer — at a different grain (@sec-mechanisms):

- **Region** (MIL max over frame cells): *where* in the frame is the referent.
- **Frame** (MIL max over a ±2 s window): *which moment* shows it best.
- **Utterance** (EM reweighting of pairs by self-estimated alignment): *which pairs* are aligned.

The oracles that bound them come from the Gemini annotation of @sec-data — a per-pair **alignment**
score and, where a visible object is named, its **referent** word. Three successively stronger
interventions build on those two labels, and it helps to state up front what each one physically
does to the training data (the mechanics and exact numbers are in @sec-label). All three operate on
the **~9% of pairs Gemini marks as referentially aligned** (~84k of 911k):

1. **Alignment filter** — throw away the other 91% and train only on the aligned pairs, keeping
   their natural utterances. This isolates *which pairs*.
2. **Word selection** — on those same aligned pairs, replace the whole utterance with just the
   referent noun, for the **~63%** of them where that noun is actually spoken in the utterance.
   This isolates *which word* names the object.
3. **Vision-binding** — additionally supply the referent noun for the remaining **~37%**, where it
   is never said aloud and so could only be recovered by *seeing* the object. This isolates the
   referent *when it is unspoken*.

Each is an oracle because it uses a label — alignment, or the referent word — that a learner has no
access to at training time.

## The ladder

![The bootstrapping ladder. Green rungs are **free** — achievable with no labels — and chain
cumulatively; blue rungs are **oracles** — upper bounds that require alignment or referent labels we
do not have at training time. The oracle rungs are an **alternative branch** out of the region-MIL
baseline (62.6), *not* stacked on frame-MIL: the guide line marks where they leave the free chain,
so the alignment filter's +5.9 is measured from region-MIL, not from the frame-MIL rung just below
it. Perfect labels cannot exceed ~81 on these frozen features.](figures/fig_waterfall_ladder.png){#fig-ladder width=95%}

The Δ column below reads the same way: free rungs are measured from the rung above, the oracle
branch from region-MIL. The **from** column makes the base explicit.

| Rung | Konkle | Δ | from | kind |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| chance | 25 | — | — | — |
| pure learning (whole-frame, noisy data) | 52.9 ± 1.7 | +27.9 | chance | free |
| **+ region MIL** | 62.6 ± 1.7 | **+9.7** | pure learning | free |
| **+ frame MIL (±2 s)** | 65.0 ± 1.8 | **+2.4** | region MIL | free |
| **+ frame MIL (±5 s)** | 66.8 ± 0.6 | **+1.8** | frame ±2 s | free |
| + alignment filter | 68.5 ± 1.3 | +5.9 | region MIL | oracle |
| + word selection | 73.2 ± 1.2 | +4.7 | filter | oracle |
| + vision-binding | 81.3 ± 2.6 | +8.1 | word selection | oracle |
| ceiling | ~81 | — | — | unlearnable from these features |

Two facts frame everything. **The free gains are large and get you most of the way:** pure
contrastive learning on noisy data already reaches 52.9, region MIL adds +9.7, and frame MIL a
further +2.4 at a ±2 s window (+4.2 at ±5 s), landing an **unaided** learner at **66.8**. Above
that, every rung is an **oracle** — it needs information (which pairs are aligned; which word is the
referent) we cannot access at training time. **No self-supervised mechanism we tried climbs those
oracle rungs.**

But the free route comes remarkably close to the first one. The alignment-filter oracle and the
free frame-MIL are **two branches out of the same region-MIL node**, both doing the same job —
isolating the referential moment — one with the Gemini alignment label, one for free by max-pooling
over space and a ±5 s window. The oracle reaches 68.5; the **free route reaches 66.8, a gap of only
1.7**. Region max-pooling already does implicit alignment selection (@sec-mechanisms), and widening
the frame window lets it reach for moments a ±2 s window misses, so self-supervised selection
recovers most of what the oracle filter provides — the referential *moment* is largely learnable
without the label. It is the referential *word*, the two rungs above, that stays out of reach.

## What the bootstraps buy

![The three self-supervised bootstraps. Region and frame selection are real, free gains; the
utterance EM bootstrap is null within seed noise.](figures/fig_waterfall_mechanisms.png){#fig-mechanisms width=80%}

**Region MIL (+9.7)** is the single largest free gain. Scoring the utterance against the
best-matching cell of a frame — with no detector and no labels — does implicit referent
*localization*, and it lands the unaided learner most of the way to the oracle filter on its own.

::: {.callout-note}
## A caveat on the size of this rung
The +9.7 here is measured against the DINOv2 **CLS token** as the whole-frame baseline (52.9), and
CLS is a *weak* object readout for DINOv2. Against a **mean-pooled** whole-frame baseline — the
fairer "no spatial selection" summary — DINOv2 whole-frame is already ~61, so region-MIL's honest
gain is closer to **+4**. Most of the apparent +9.7 is CLS being a poor summary, not spatial
selection being powerful, and the gain shrinks further for stronger encoders. @sec-encoders works
this out across encoders; the ladder here is kept on the CLS baseline for internal consistency with
the rest of the chapter.
:::

**Frame MIL (+2.4)** is a modest but consistent free gain. A region × frame $2\times2$ isolates it:

| | single frame | + frame MIL (±2 s) |
|---|---|---|
| whole-frame | 52.9 ± 1.7 | 55.5 ± 1.7 (+2.6) |
| region | 62.6 ± 1.7 | **65.0 ± 1.8 (+2.4)** |

Selecting the best *moment* in a short window adds ~+2.4 on top of region selection (positive in
all three seeds), roughly additive with region's +9.7. Which-moment matters, a little, on top of
which-region.

### How wide should the window be?

Frame MIL has one free parameter — how much time around the utterance the learner is allowed to
look over. Widening it trades off two things: a longer window is more likely to *contain* the
referential moment, but it also dilutes the selection with more off-target frames. We can just
measure it, holding region MIL fixed and stretching the window from a single frame to ±2 s to ±5 s
(at 1 fps, 5 and 11 candidate frames):

| window | candidate frames | Konkle test-60 (3 seeds) | Δ vs. prev |
|---|---|---|---|
| single frame | 1 | 62.6 ± 1.7 | — |
| ±2 s | 5 | 65.0 ± 1.8 | +2.4 |
| ±5 s | 11 | **66.8 ± 0.6** | +1.8 |

The gain is **monotone with diminishing returns**: each widening still helps, by a little less. At
±5 s the containment benefit is still winning over the dilution cost — the referential moment is
often just outside a ±2 s window, and letting the max reach for it recovers another ~+1.8. But the
curve is clearly bending, and ±5 s is already 11 frames of a 1 fps stream; there is no regime change
waiting at a wider window, only a slow approach to whatever the region-MIL selection can extract.
This ±5 s value — **66.8**, the top of the free chain in the ladder — is what closes most of the
gap to the alignment-filter oracle (68.5): the extra temporal reach is exactly the free mechanism
catching moments the oracle filter would have kept.

**Utterance EM is null.** The self-supervised EM loop — reweighting pairs by the model's own
max-region alignment, the direct attempt to climb the *filter* rung without the oracle — does
essentially nothing:

| | −EM | +EM | effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| whole-frame | 52.9 ± 1.7 | 53.6 ± 2.3 | +0.7 |
| region | 62.6 ± 1.7 | 63.8 ± 2.3 | +1.2 |

Both effects sit inside the seed noise (sd ≈ 2). This is a firm version of "the bootstrap does not
ignite": pair-reweighting by the model's own alignment estimate is indistinguishable from zero —
and region MIL has already absorbed most of what it targets.

## The label decomposition {#sec-label}

Here are the mechanics behind the three oracle interventions previewed at the start of the chapter.
They are built to be *nested*, so their gains add up cleanly. We start from the **83,794 referentially-aligned pairs**
— the ~9% of the 910,975 training pairs to which Gemini assigned a visible referent — and hold that
pair set fixed. The only thing that changes across the three rungs is the **text** each pair is
trained against:

- **filtered-natural** — the aligned pairs with their *natural utterance* unchanged ("*look, is
  that a doggie?*"). This is the alignment filter of the main ladder, restated on the
  referent-bearing set.
- **referent word *where spoken*** — for each pair, if the referent noun actually appears in the
  utterance, we throw the rest of the sentence away and train on the bare noun ("*dog*"); otherwise
  we leave the utterance untouched. The referent turns out to be spoken in **63%** of these aligned
  pairs, so this rewrites 63% of them and leaves 37% as natural text.
- **referent word *always*** — we supply the bare referent noun for **all** the pairs, including the
  37% where it was never said.

The three differ only in text, on identical frames and identical pairs, so each Δ isolates one thing
(@fig-label).

![Where the label headroom lives: filtering to referential pairs, selecting the spoken referent
word, and — the largest single piece — supplying the referent when it is *not* spoken at all.
](figures/fig_waterfall_label.png){#fig-label width=80%}

| step | Konkle | Δ | isolates |
|---|---|---|---|
| region-MIL baseline | 62.6 | — | — |
| filtered-natural | 68.5 | +5.9 | which pairs |
| referent word *where spoken* | 73.2 | +4.7 | which word |
| referent word *always* | 81.3 | +8.1 | referent when unspoken (vision) |

Why is the referent spoken in as many as **63%** of aligned pairs, when only ~9% of *all* pairs are
aligned in the first place? Because the 63% is conditional on alignment: it is 63% *of the ~9%*, not
63% overall. And it is high for exactly the reason those pairs were kept — Gemini calls a pair
aligned when the caregiver is talking about a visible object, and most of the time naming that
object is *why* they are talking about it, so its noun is right there in the transcript. The other
37% are still genuinely aligned — the caregiver is attending to the visible object — but they refer
to it without the noun: deixis and pronouns ("*look at **that**!*", "*pick **it** up*"), or a
description ("*is it yummy?*"). Those pairs carry a real referential moment but no referential
*word*.

That split is what makes the last two rungs mean different things. Supplying the noun for the
*spoken* 63% (word selection, +4.7) mostly buys **disambiguation** — pulling the referent out of a
sentence that also contains other content words. Supplying it for the *unspoken* 37%
(vision-binding, +8.1) is the single largest piece, because for those pairs the noun is *new
information*: it cannot be read off the language at all, only off the image. This is why @sec-cues
aims accessible cues at *identifying the referent* — including visually, when it isn't said — rather
than merely filtering frames.

## Synthesis

The unaided learner reaches **66.8** — bought by pure learning and the two free MIL selections
(region, and frame at a ±5 s window). That lands it within **1.7** of the alignment-filter oracle:
free spatial + temporal selection nearly matches what the oracle *which-pairs* label provides,
because region max-pooling over a wide window already isolates the referential moment on its own.
The oracle rungs that stay out of reach are the two above it — **which word** names the object, and
**which object** is named when no word is spoken. Everything from there to the **81** ceiling is an
oracle, and the one self-supervised attempt to climb it (utterance EM) is null. So the bottleneck is
not optimization or scale, and it is no longer really *which moment* either — it is **which
referent**: the object being named, especially when it is never spoken. The next chapter asks
whether the cues children actually use can supply any of it.
